episodes.label: Episode 1

semantics.summary: Student implemented size() and height() methods, establishing the foundation for tree property queries. First successful tests pass for tree height/size computation.

episodes.outcome: testIsEmpty went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 2

semantics.summary: Student implemented isEmpty() and began working on containsNonBST(). isEmpty() passed quickly, but containsNonBST() proved challenging with multiple unsuccessful debugging attempts (runs 3-8) showing trial-and-error approach without clear understanding of the non-BST traversal algorithm. Finally achieved breakthrough in run 9 when containsNonBST() passed.

episodes.outcome: testContainsNonBST went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 3

semantics.summary: Student implemented toString() method, getting the basic version working. Then encountered a StackOverflowError from infinite recursion in the toString logic, which was partially fixed but left formatting issues (missing spaces between elements).

episodes.outcome: testBasicToString went from passing to failing

episodes.label: Episode 4

semantics.summary: Student fixed the toString() formatting issue (adding proper spacing after commas) and then successfully implemented toArrayList(). Both toString and toArrayList categories now fully passing.

episodes.outcome: testBasicToString went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 5

semantics.summary: Student implemented toArray() method, successfully converting the tree to an array representation. Quick incremental addition building on the working toArrayList() implementation.

episodes.outcome: testToString went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 6

semantics.summary: Student implemented inefficientIterator() and began working on preOrderIterator(). The inefficient iterator passed immediately, but preOrderIterator() required extensive debugging across multiple runs (19-25) with evolving errors: hasNext() logic issues, null returns, wrong traversal order, and missing NoSuchElementException handling. Finally achieved breakthrough when preOrderIterator() passed.

episodes.outcome: testPreOrderIterator went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 7

semantics.summary: Student tackled the in-order iterator implementation, which proved to be the most challenging feature. After initial NullPointerException on uninitialized fields (run 26), the student entered an extended debugging plateau (runs 27-40) with persistent null return values and incorrect traversal order. Error messages slowly evolved from null returns to wrong values to hasNext() logic issues before finally achieving a breakthrough in run 40.

episodes.outcome: testIterator went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 8

semantics.summary: Major transition from manual testing to full automated test suite. Student unlocked insert category tests and quickly added exception handling for null insert arguments, passing edge_cases category. Then encountered a compilation error (unreachable code in contains()) while implementing additional features, which was quickly fixed to achieve 27/27 tests passing.

episodes.outcome: testInsertExceptions went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 9

semantics.summary: Student unlocked efficiency tests and began implementing remove() method. Efficiency tests passed but all three remove tests failed, indicating the remove skeleton was in place but logic was incomplete.

episodes.outcome: testContainsInts went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 10

semantics.summary: Extended debugging session on remove() implementation. Started with stalled progress and a test infrastructure breakdown (run 47-48), recovered the test suite, then achieved partial success with testRemove() and testRemoveReturnValue() passing. However, testRemoveAdvanced() remained failing (wrong node count after removal), suggesting issues with the two-children removal case. Multiple stalled runs at the end indicate the student was stuck on this edge case.

episodes.outcome: testRemove went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 11

semantics.summary: Student attempted to fix testRemoveAdvanced() but caused a major regression: all three remove tests now fail with wildly incorrect size values (expected 4 but got 14), indicating remove() was no longer actually removing nodes from the tree.

episodes.outcome: testRemove went from passing to failing

episodes.label: Episode 12

semantics.summary: Student continued struggling with remove() implementation, initially worsening the situation with a StackOverflowError from infinite recursion (run 54). Then achieved the final breakthrough in run 55: all three remove tests passed, completing the entire assignment with 33/33 tests across all 14 categories. Runs 56-57 confirmed stability of the solution.

episodes.outcome: testRemove went from failing to passing

semantics.summary: Final verification and potential refactoring session. All 33 tests remain passing with no regressions. Student confirmed complete assignment stability after the remove() breakthrough.

feedback.pattern: Regression from incorrect two-children removal logic
feedback.explanation: This test (along with testRemove()) covers BST removal correctness, including verifying that remove() returns the correct boolean and that the tree structure remains valid. The test first passed at run 50 after a critical fix: changing from calling `removeHelper(root, i, b)` without capturing the return value to `root = removeHelper(root, i, b)`, which ensures the root pointer is updated when the root node itself is removed. However, at run 53, the two-children case logic was rewritten — the code switched from finding the in-order predecessor (go left, then right) to finding the in-order successor (go right, then left), and also changed how the replacement node's children were reassigned. This produced incorrect size values (expected 4 but got 14/15), indicating nodes were not being properly detached. At run 54, the error messages flipped (expected 14 but got 4), indicating the logic still did not correctly splice the successor into place. At run 55, the two-children case was substantially rewritten — introducing a `prev` pointer to track the parent of the successor, a comparison-based while loop to find the correct in-order successor, and a conditional check (`bottom != cur.left`) to handle the case where the successor is the immediate child — and all three remove tests passed through run 57.
nextSteps: The three-case BST removal pattern (leaf, one child, two children via in-order successor) recurs directly in EditorTrees Milestone 3's delete(int pos), which adds AVL rebalancing on top; solidify your understanding of why the successor's parent must have its child pointer updated to the successor's right subtree before the successor replaces the deleted node.

Practice the pointer-replacement pattern where recursive helpers return the (possibly updated) node reference so the parent automatically re-links: `node.left = removeHelper(node.left, ...)`. This eliminates the need for separate parent-tracking in many cases and is less error-prone than iterative splicing.

When removing a node with two children, always verify your logic handles the edge case where the in-order successor (or predecessor) is the immediate child of the node being removed — this case requires different pointer updates than when the successor is deeper in the subtree.

feedback.explanation: The in-order iterator failed across runs 26–39 before passing at run 40. The initial NullPointerException at run 26 was caused by an uninitialized field. After that was fixed, the test failed with AssertionFailedError for 13 runs, with error messages showing wrong values (1 instead of 2), null returns, and other incorrect outputs — all indicating the stack-based traversal logic did not correctly simulate the recursive in-order pattern. The fix at run 40 involved a significant rework of the `next()` method: the flag value pushed when descending left was changed from 1 to 2 (indicating the node has been visited for its left subtree), and new logic was added to pop a node, check if it has a right child, and conditionally push the right child with a fresh flag of 1 while correctly deciding whether to re-push the current node. The implementation distinguishes between three states: a node being visited for the first time (explore left), being returned as the current value (after left subtree is done), and needing its right subtree explored — managed via the flags stack.
nextSteps: The in-order traversal pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must traverse a rank-ordered tree in O(N); make sure you can articulate why in-order visits nodes in sorted order for a BST and how the stack replaces the call stack's role in recursion.

For stack-based in-order traversal, a cleaner approach than multi-state flags is: push all left descendants onto the stack initially, then on each `next()` call, pop the top node, return its value, and push all left descendants of its right child. This two-phase pattern avoids the complexity of tracking visit states.

feedback.pattern: Stuck on AssertionFailedError with eventual StackOverflowError
feedback.explanation: testRemoveAdvanced() tests more complex removal scenarios (likely involving nodes with two children in various tree configurations) and failed across runs 45–54 before passing at run 55. While testRemove() and testRemoveReturnValue() passed at run 50 after capturing the return value of `removeHelper`, this advanced test continued to fail with assertion errors through run 53, indicating the two-children removal case had a logic error that manifested with certain tree structures. At run 53, the code was changed to use in-order successor traversal (go right, then left) but with incorrect pointer reassignment, causing size mismatches. At run 54, a StackOverflowError occurred, indicating the removal logic created a cycle in the tree (a node pointing back to an ancestor), causing infinite recursion on subsequent operations. The fix at run 55 introduced a `prev` pointer to properly track the successor's parent, used a comparison-based loop to find the correct in-order successor, and added a conditional branch (`bottom != cur.left`) to handle the case where the successor is the immediate child differently from when it's deeper in the subtree.
nextSteps: In EditorTrees Milestone 3, delete(int pos) uses the same three-case removal logic plus AVL rebalancing; the two-children case requires finding the in-order successor, copying its data into the node being deleted, and then recursively removing the successor from its original position — this recursive approach avoids the pointer-splicing bugs you encountered.

When implementing the two-children case iteratively, draw out the pointer changes for both sub-cases: (1) the successor is the immediate right child of the deleted node, and (2) the successor is deeper in the left subtree of the right child. The StackOverflowError at run 54 indicates a circular reference was created, which happens when you reassign child pointers without accounting for which sub-case you're in.

Consider using the 'copy and delete' strategy for two-children removal: copy the successor's data into the current node, then recursively delete the successor from the right subtree. This reduces the two-children case to a one-child or leaf case and avoids manual pointer manipulation entirely.

feedback.pattern: Stuck on AssertionFailedError for 6 consecutive runs
feedback.explanation: The containsNonBST() method — which searches the entire tree rather than exploiting BST ordering — failed from run 1 through run 8 with the same assertion error (returning false when the element exists in the tree), then passed at run 9. The initial implementation at run 3 compiled but had a logic error in the recursive traversal. Across runs 3–8, six consecutive assertion failures occurred with the same error message. The fix at run 9 added 20 lines including a proper recursive structure. The key difference between containsNonBST() and a BST-optimized contains() is that containsNonBST() must search both left and right subtrees at every node (since the tree may not satisfy the BST property), returning true if either subtree contains the target. A common implementation error is returning the result of only one recursive branch or not properly combining the boolean results from left and right subtrees with an OR operation.
nextSteps: The left-or-right navigation pattern used in BST contains() recurs in Exam 2's shortestWordAlongPath, which follows the same comparison-based path but accumulates data along the way; make sure you understand the distinction between BST-optimized search (O(log n), one path) and exhaustive tree search (O(n), all paths).

For any tree search that must visit all nodes, the recursive pattern is: check the current node, then return `searchLeft(node.left) || searchRight(node.right)` — short-circuit evaluation means you stop as soon as one branch returns true. Ensure your base case returns false for NULL_NODE.
Practice writing both iterative (using a queue or stack) and recursive versions of full-tree search to build fluency with tree traversal patterns that don't rely on BST ordering.

feedback.pattern: Stuck on AssertionFailedError for 6 consecutive runs
feedback.explanation: The pre-order iterator failed across runs 19–24 with assertion errors that changed in character: at run 19 hasNext() returned wrong values, at run 22 next() returned null, and at run 23 next() returned elements in wrong order (7 instead of 5). The fix at run 25 was a substantial 25-line addition that addressed multiple issues: the root was now conditionally pushed only if it wasn't NULL_NODE (preventing errors on empty trees), a version field was added for concurrent modification detection, and the stack management in next() was corrected. Pre-order traversal with a stack requires pushing the right child before the left child (so left is processed first due to LIFO order), and the error at run 23 (returning 7 instead of 5) is consistent with pushing children in the wrong order or not pushing the root first.
nextSteps: Pre-order traversal order (root, left, right) is central to EditorTrees toString() and HW6's preOrderInOrderBuild, which reconstructs a tree from its pre-order string; internalize that pre-order always visits the root before any descendants, making it natural for serialization and reconstruction.

For a stack-based pre-order iterator, the algorithm is: pop the top node, return its value, then push its right child followed by its left child (right first so left is on top). This is simpler than in-order iteration because there's no need to track visit states — each node is processed exactly once when popped.

Always guard against pushing NULL_NODE onto the stack — check `if (node.right != NULL_NODE)` before pushing. This simplifies hasNext() to just checking `!stack.isEmpty()` and prevents null-related errors.
